Here’s how to make your storytelling so addictive, it is basically impossible to skip.

This is called the Triad of Addicting Stories.

There’s only 3 elements, but if you nail all 3, your stories will be top 1%.

All addicting stories answer yes to these 3 questions…

1. (Relevant) Is it something I care about?
2. (Novel) Is it a new concept I’ve never heard before?
3. (Interesting) Am I intrigued to want to learn more?

These map to relevant, novel and interesting.

Here’s how to incorporate each one in your stories.

“Is it something I care about?” is relevance.

And this one is the easiest.

Only pick topics you know your ideal viewer already cares about.

To make sure it feels relevant, you could call them out directly by name in the hook, or introduce a painpoint you know they have.

Now for the second piece, “is it a new concept I’ve never heard before…this is novelty.

To make your stories feel novel, you either need to be the first to say something new, or wrap something old in a new frame.

Something new could be a news event, an update, or a freshly published story.

These are easy to win with but hard to find first unless you’re looking outside of your native medium.

Wrapping something old in a new frame takes more creativity but is always available because there are infinite twists to be made on an old topic.

Now the last question is “Am I intrigued to want to learn more”

And this solves for interestingness.

For entertainment content, this comes down to the stakes you build for the character.

If the stakes feel extreme, intrigue goes up.

For education content, this comes down to the painpoint or outcome you’re talking about.

The closer your story connects to a pain they have our outcome they want, the more interested they will be

What you say, what you show visually, and what you write in the hook must complement each other perfectly.

If you want to improve your storytelling, this is the #1 psychology trick.

Comment “story” and I’ll send through my entire short-form storytelling template database.

Every one of these videos…got millions of views, and they all used it in different ways.

It’s called…Anticipation Loading.

Here’s how it works.

Your brain releases the most dopamine right before an answer is revealed.

This means the longer someone is kept guessing…the more hooked they’ll be and the longer they’ll watch.

This is why mystery novels and crime shows are so addicting.

The answer is buried until the end.

Now most people understand this, but they aren’t using it correctly in their content.

So here’s how to do it…

Start by making a hook that pops a relevant question in the viewer’s mind.

This could be a direct question you say or some visual that gets the viewer wondering what might happen next.

This is the initial anticipation.

Then, do everything you can to build more tension on top of that open question.

Examples, proof, subplots anything that ratchets up the stakes without revealing the answer.

This is called the loading.

The longer you can make them wait, the better your video will do.

But here’s the real secret sauce.

Once you do reveal the answer, try to engage them again by opening another loop.

This will reset their curiosity and give you a second chance at building even more anticipation.

If you do this 2-3 times throughout a video, your retention will be through the roof.

Here’s how to make your storytelling so good, it is scientifically impossible to scroll away.

What you’re missing is a rehook.

But not just any rehook…the Mid Flip Rehook.

And this one thing will dramatically extend your watch time.

Here’s how it works…

The attention span for most short-form content is about 25 seconds.

That means, if you don’t use a Mid Flip around the 25 second mark, most of your viewers will scroll away.

For example, right about now, you’re wondering if you should keep watching this video.

And that’s because the sand in your attention hourglass is about to run out.

So let me just get to the good part…

This is how you actually create the Mid Flip Rehook in your video.

First you want to figure out the core contrarian insight you’re basing the video around.

And you build the first 20 seconds of the video on that.

So for this video, my core insight was the fact that you needed a rehook to hold attention.

And not just any rehook…a Mid Flip Rehook.

Now that initial take and brief explanation…is great, but it will only hold about 20 seconds of your attention.

So then, I need to figure out another valuable segment for the back-half of the video.

And what I chose was to explain in depth how to make the Mid Life.

So the first half was “what it is” and the second half was “how to make it”

Now the Mid Flip Rehook is the transitional moment where you shift from part 1 to part 2.

And you do it, in such a way that it opens a new curiosity loop for the viewer.

This is what resets the hourglass.

The best way to do it, is by using a contrasting word…but, however, although, things like that.

It’s called a Mid Flip because it’s literally like I flip the hourglass of your attention in the middle of the video to buy myself 25 more seconds.

And now you watched the entire thing.

Not having a Mid Flip is 1 of the core 7 storytelling mistakes beginners make that prevent their videos from crushing.

The reason your videos are not working is because the viewers are suffering from Flashbang Brain.

This is the #1 reason why content is so hard now

When you scroll even 2 videos from now, your memory of what I’m currently saying will be completely gone.

As if a flashbang went off in your head and reset your brain completely.

That is Flashbang brain.

Now this means, any of the information I said, or perspective I shared, literally goes in one ear and out the ear.

And so long-term trust doesn’t accrue.

This is why it’s so hard to build a following…people literally do not remember you 30 seconds after they see you.

So here’s what you do…

There are two ways to shift your content strategy once you realize flashbang brain is a problem.

Number 1 is to design every video like an off-ramp.

You have to assume viewers have never seen you before and after they watch this one video, they will never see you again.

So because of that, you want to ramp as many of them as possible from the chaos of the feed to a much slower medium.

Slower than the feed could be your profile, email, long-form video, or a private community.

If social feeds are running the brain at 100mph, we gotta ramp them down to something slower to have a better chance of them remembering us.

Now, shift #2 is to make every video with the sole objective of either conversion or binging. 

Every time I make a video, I’m aiming to either collect a lead, via email, or to compel the viewer to binge 10 more videos on my profile right away.

1 video isn’t enough to overcome the Flashbang brain, but 10 in a row might be.

And to do this, that means the bingeability rails in your content, whether through a series, S-tier information, or just insane visuals, needs to compel them to click your profile and binge.

Now this Flashbang brain problem is the number 1 issue making it harder to grow.

This is the easiest storytelling hack for improving educational content.

It’s called Embedded Truths.

When you write scripts, you wanna frame your statements as if they were already true.

For example, stop saying, “If you want that result, you should do this thing”...

Instead say, “Do this thing to get that result.”

You’re shifting from wishy washy “if, then” language to much more declarative language.

Now this sounds like a small tweak, but it will have a massive impact on your video’s performance.

Here’s why…

When viewers watch educational content, their subconscious brain is trying to assess trust and certainty.

They don’t want to learn things that “might” get them a result.

They want to hear things that for sure will get them the result.

Declarative speech signals much higher confidence and they will trust you way quicker because of it.

These are 6 levels of storytelling you can use to make a video.

It’s called the Story Ladder.

And the higher you’re able to go up this ladder, the more addicting your stories will be.

The Level 1 Storyteller is called The Reporter.

This is where you include the core facts in the story, but you state them in a super predictable order.

The Level 2 Storyteller is called The Illusionist.

This where in addition to the core facts, you also add hooks to the intro and body of the video.

If you can do this a couple times in the story, you’re at level 2.

The Level 3 Storyteller is called The Champion.

This is where you keep the core facts and hooks, but now you also add stakes.

Stakes are the use cases, problems, or individual characters that make a viewer feel personally connected to the story.

From here, we’re getting into advanced mode.

The Level 4 Storyteller is called The Architect.

And this is where you start adding arcs and loops into your story.

Arcs are like waves where you add and release tension throughout…to create more rhythm in the pacing.

Loops are like mini subplots that open and close.

The Level 5 Storyteller is called The Translator.

At this level, you’re taking everything from the first 4 levels, and then trying to add additional comprehension and clarity so that the viewer is 100% clear at all times.

Lastly is Level 6…The Maestro.

This is all about adding the sauce and your unique fingerprint to the story.

This is your signature style or the 1 of 1 thing that makes you unique.

Here’s how to make your stories 10x more interesting in 60 seconds.

It’s called, The Shock Score.

The best stories all have one thing in common…headfakes.

Something shocking, unexpected, or super non-obvious.

For entertainment content, this is called a Misdirection.

But for education content, this is called a Contrarian Take.

Now the reason your stories don’t hold attention, is because you’re not coming up with strong enough headfakes.

And just solving this one thing will make your stories so much more compelling.

So here’s how to do it…

First, start with the baseline facts you’ve already shared in your story.

For entertainment, this is whatever the character has done up to this point.

For education, these are the facts you’ve already introduced.

Now second, list out all the possible things that could happen next.

And ask yourself this one question…

If I had 100 people in a room, how many of them would be shocked if this is what I said?

That number is your shock score.

A shock score of 90 means that 90 out of 100 people would have not seen your headfake coming.

The higher the Shock Score, the bigger the headfake, and the more interesting your story will be.

Now in entertainment content this is pretty obvious, but in education content this is the secret behind why certain personal brands scale so quickly.

They consistently deliver non-obvious contrarian takes that shock the viewer and hold their attention.

Headfakes are 1 of the core 8 storytelling principles that make for winning videos.

The reason your videos are flopping is because you’re making these 3 mistakes in your hook.

These are called Skip Rate Ruiners.

#1 is the length of your first two sentences.

And this’ll sound way too simple to matter, but it’s actually huge.

The more words you say per sentence, especially in the hook, the worse your video will do.

This is called overloading.

The brain can only absorb so many words at once, while keeping a memory of what has already been said.

Longer sentences are harder to retain, which drives confusion and churn.

Make your first two sentences a max of 10-15 words and your views will go way up.

#2 is called a proof loop.

And this is super important for educational content specifically.

If you make a bold claim in your hook, you need to add some proof right away to validate that claim is true.

It could be your own numbers, a 3rd party study, or someone else’s results…but having proof drives retention way up.

The proof loop is the question cycle that pops in the viewer’s head.

Is that claim true?
Okay, Is that proof legit?
Okay I believe you, tell me more.

Without the proof, the churn will go up.

#3 is the double hook, sometimes called the rehook.

If you tee up the hook well initially, a base curiosity loop should open in the viewer’s brain wanting to know more.

Within the first 15 seconds, your goal is to hook them again using additional contrast.

Essentially, adding another headfake, another open loop, or more intrigue.

This deepens the curiosity significantly more than just having the base hook.

Here’s how to write a hook so good it is scientifically impossible to skip.

This is called the Triple Hook Method.

And if you do this right, it will hypnotize the viewer in a way where they physically cannot scroll away.

Step 1 is the Context.

This is the basic step, but so many people still get this wrong.

Viewers only watch content where they have a vested interest in the topic.

So the first line of the hook must establish context on what the video will be about.

You can say it in the audio, show it in the visuals, write it in the text or caption, ideally all 3 aligned, but this context must be established immediately.

We’ve have data that shows even delaying context towards the end of the first sentence causes the skip rate to go way up.

So priority number 1 is to set immediate context.

Now Step 2 is where most people mess up.

This is the lean.

What you’re trying to do is get someone curious in a certain direction.

You want them to lean in on the context and actively want to hear more.

Now you can make this lean happen in a variety of ways…

But regardless of which method you pick, the viewer must lean in and not opt out.

So when you read back that first 1-2 sentences on its own…is the context clear and is there something curiosity inducing that would make you lean in and want to hear more?

Context Lean…this is what “opens the curiosity loop” you hear people talk about.

Now step 3 is really where the money’s made.

I call this, the Contrarian Snapback.

To catch a fish, you get the hook in its mouth swimming one way, and then you jerk back the other way.

Not to be morbid.

Storytelling is the same way.

The goal is to say something that pulls the viewer away from the direction they were just leaning.

Essentially, snapping them back down another path.

Is the god-tier hook formula that works every single time.
